strengths: Addresses an important and practical task, software issue localization, with an efficient retrieve-and-rerank framework that avoids the high cost and latency of agent-based systems.

Introduces SweLoc, a large-scale GitHub-derived dataset for issue localization, with consistency filtering and hard-negative mining; demonstrates its utility by improving multiple retriever and reranker models.

Reports strong and comprehensive empirical results on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, outperforming prior ranking models and several costly agent-based systems using closed-source LLMs such as Claude-3.5.
Provides useful ablations on data filtering threshold K and training data size, and offers a cost-effectiveness analysis showing favorable accuracy/cost trade-offs.
Technical approach is reasonably sound: contrastive bi-encoder retrieval with mined hard negatives and an adapted listwise LLM reranker trained from single-positive supervision.
weaknesses: The framework is largely a task-specific application of existing retrieve-and-rerank components plus dataset construction; novelty is mostly empirical rather than architectural or algorithmic.

The reranker training objective only supervises the positive identifier and omits the end-of-sequence token, which is somewhat ad hoc and leaves unclear how issues with multiple positive functions and full listwise inference are handled consistently.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully controlled: agent-based results are taken from prior work, GPT-4.1 is competitive or better on several metrics, and candidate pools/costs across methods may differ.

Dataset/code availability is not clearly stated in the provided manuscript, and reproducibility is weakened by missing explicit release details and limited discussion of pretraining data contamination or leakage risks.
Evaluation is restricted to Python repositories and two benchmarks; there are no variance estimates or statistical significance tests, and the SWE-Bench-Lite evaluation subset is relatively small.
The cost analysis focuses on reranker/agent inference cost and may not fully account for retrieval indexing or end-to-end pipeline costs.

strengths: Introduces SWELOC, a large-scale dataset for software issue localization curated from public GitHub repositories, with consistency filtering and hard-negative mining, and demonstrates its utility for fine-tuning multiple retrievers and rerankers.

Proposes SWERANK, a practical retrieve-and-rerank framework that achieves strong empirical results on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, outperforming several agent-based baselines and prior ranking models on many metrics.
Shows substantial inference cost savings compared to agent-based systems using closed-source LLMs, making the approach attractive for practical deployment.
Provides detailed training setup and hyperparameters, supporting reproducibility to some extent.
Evaluates localization at multiple granularities (file, module, function) and across difficulty categories in LocBench.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the framework combines existing bi-encoder and listwise LLM reranker architectures with a new dataset; dataset construction largely follows the established SWE-Bench pipeline, and the reranker training objective is only a minor adaptation.

Dataset labels are automatically derived from all functions modified in a pull request, which may include irrelevant changes (e.g., refactoring, style, tests); consistency filtering using CodeRankEmbed may introduce selection bias, and there is no human validation or error analysis of dataset quality.

Evaluation comparisons are potentially unfair: agent-based baselines are not re-run on the same filtered evaluation set (e.g., 274 vs original SWE-Bench-Lite examples), and numbers are taken directly from prior work; GPT-4.1 outperforms SWERANKLLM-LARGE on several reported metrics, contradicting the broad SOTA claim.

The reranker is trained only to predict the positive identifier rather than a full ranking, and it is unclear how full ranked lists are generated at inference; no ablation compares this simplified objective against standard full listwise training.

Cost analysis considers only inference cost, ignoring the substantial training cost (e.g., 32B model on 16 GH200 GPUs) and retriever index construction cost, which undermines the claimed cost-effectiveness.
Missing statistical significance and variance across runs; final SWELOC dataset size, licensing, and ethical considerations for using public GitHub data are not adequately discussed.
The abstract and introduction contain overclaims about outperforming closed-source models that are not supported across all metrics or granularities.
Minor clarity issues and typos throughout (e.g., "retrieve-and-erank", inconsistent capitalization of SWERANK).

strengths: Addresses an important and practically costly problem—software issue localization—with an efficient retrieve-and-rerank framework that avoids expensive closed-source agentic pipelines.

Introduces SweLoc, a large-scale issue-localization dataset built from real GitHub PRs with consistency filtering and hard-negative mining, and convincingly demonstrates its utility by fine-tuning a variety of retrievers and rerankers.

Reports strong empirical results on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, achieving state-of-the-art file/module/function localization and outperforming agent-based methods such as LocAgent with Claude-3.5, while offering markedly better cost efficiency.
Includes a solid set of experiments: data filtering ablations, data-size scaling, multiple base model choices, and a cost analysis that supports the main practical claims.
The paper is well written, with clear task motivation and sufficient training details in the appendix for the proposed models.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is limited: retrieve-and-rerank, contrastive bi-encoder training, and listwise LLM reranking are well-established techniques; the main contribution is largely the dataset and application-specific training.

The reranker training objective is simplified to predicting only the positive identifier and uses sampled negatives, rather than top-K retrieved candidates, creating a potential train/inference mismatch and limiting evidence that full listwise ranking supervision is unnecessary.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: the assertion that SweRank exceeds closed-source models across all metrics is not fully supported, as GPT-4.1 remains better on several file/module/function metrics in the tables.
The agent-based baseline numbers are taken from prior work rather than reimplemented under a controlled setup, and evaluation is restricted to Python repositories, which may limit generalizability.
Reproducibility is only partially addressed: no explicit code/dataset release link is provided, and licensing/consent considerations for the mined GitHub data are not discussed.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem: software issue localization from verbose natural-language issue descriptions, where existing code ranking models are not well optimized and agentic methods are costly.

Introduces SweLoc, a large-scale contrastive dataset curated from real GitHub pull requests, with consistency filtering and hard-negative mining; the paper shows the dataset improves multiple retriever and reranker models across model families.
Proposes SweRank, a retrieve-and-rerank framework with SweRankEmbed (bi-encoder) and SweRankLLM (listwise LLM reranker), achieving state-of-the-art localization on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench.

Provides extensive empirical analysis: data quality and size effects, retriever and reranker finetuning, inference cost, issue complexity, lexical/semantic overlap, multilingual generalization, and downstream repair performance.
Demonstrates strong practical advantages: substantially lower inference cost and latency than agentic baselines, use of open-source models, and improved downstream issue resolution on SWE-Bench-Lite.
Clear writing and well-organized presentation, with useful appendices on training details, ablations, retrieval ceiling, token efficiency, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: retrieve-and-rerank and listwise LLM reranking are established techniques; the main contribution is the task-specific dataset and its application to issue localization.

Potential selection bias: consistency filtering and hard-negative mining use CodeRankEmbed, and SweRankEmbed-Small is initialized from CodeRankEmbed, which may bias retained instances toward that model's embedding space and inflate the small retriever's reported gains.

SweRankLLM is trained only to generate the positive identifier first, while inference requires a full ranked list; there is no ablation showing whether this objective is as effective as full-list supervision or whether generated rankings beyond the first item are well-calibrated.

Dataset reporting is incomplete: the final number of training instances after filtering and the train/validation/test splits are not clearly stated in the main paper, and release/license/privacy considerations for GitHub-derived data are not discussed.

Evaluation lacks statistical significance tests or confidence intervals on relatively small test sets (274 SWE-Bench-Lite examples and 560 LocBench examples), making it harder to assess whether margins over strong baselines are robust.

Agentic baselines are largely compared using previously reported numbers rather than rerun under identical conditions, which raises potential concerns about fair comparison despite the paper's strong overall results.

The strict Acc@k metric requiring all relevant code locations within top-k may understate partial localization utility, while file/module relevance based on the maximum function score may overstate file- and module-level performance.

Cost and latency claims depend on specific hardware, pricing, and implementation assumptions that are only partially specified; broader reproducibility would benefit from more implementation and release details.

No dedicated limitations or ethics section discusses possible pretraining contamination from public GitHub issue text, dataset biases, or failure modes on out-of-distribution repositories and issue types.

strengths: Introduces SweLoc, a large-scale issue-localization dataset curated from public GitHub repositories, which is a useful resource for training and evaluating retrieval models on bug-report-to-code localization.
Demonstrates strong empirical results on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, outperforming prior code ranking models and several costly agent-based localization systems in accuracy and cost-efficiency.

Provides extensive experiments and analyses, including data filtering/size ablations, negative mining, model capacity, multilingual generalization, downstream repair impact, and complexity/lexical/semantic breakdowns.
Clear and well-organized presentation with detailed training hyperparameters and implementation choices in the appendix.
Shows practical advantages in inference cost and latency, arguing for a single-shot retrieve-and-rerank approach over multi-step agentic pipelines.
weaknesses: The central state-of-the-art claim is overstated: on SWE-Bench-Lite, GPT-4.1 as a reranker with the same retriever outperforms SweRankLLM-Large on several reported metrics (e.g., File Acc@3/5, Module Acc@5, Function Acc@5), yet it is excluded from the bolded 'best overall' results and not addressed in the abstract.

Methodological novelty is limited: the framework combines standard bi-encoder retrieval and listwise LLM reranking, while dataset construction largely follows existing recipes such as SWE-Bench and CornStack filtering/hard-negative mining. The reranker is trained only to generate the positive identifier as the first token and uses a single positive per instance, which may not directly optimize for ranking multiple relevant functions as required by the all-relevant Acc@k metric.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a dataset-centric contribution: the paper does not provide a link or access plan for SweLoc, models, or code, despite claiming the dataset is a community resource. Licensing, privacy, and consent considerations for scraping public GitHub data are not discussed.

Evaluation protocol has inconsistencies and unclear details: different Acc@k cutoffs are used across granularities (File @1/3/5, Module @5/10, Function @5/10), making cross-granularity comparisons harder. It is also unclear how the reranker, trained with a listwise window size of 10, is applied for Acc@15 on LocBench or for larger candidate sets at inference.

Cost and token-efficiency analyses lack transparent methodology, especially for open-source models where API costs are not directly applicable; this makes the performance-cost tradeoff claims harder to verify.

strengths: Addresses an important and practical problem—software issue localization—with an efficient retrieve-and-rerank alternative to costly agentic methods.

Constructs SweLoc, a large-scale issue-localization dataset from real GitHub issues with consistency filtering and hard-negative mining, and demonstrates its utility across multiple retriever and reranker models.
Reports strong empirical results on SWE-Bench-Lite and LocBench, outperforming prior ranking models and agent-based systems such as LocAgent across file, module, and function granularities.
Includes comprehensive analyses of cost, latency, token footprint, downstream repair impact, model capacity, negative mining, embedding dimension, and multilingual generalization.
The paper is generally well written and the experimental setup is clearly described, making the main claims easy to follow.
weaknesses: The core method is a standard retrieve-and-rerank pipeline; the main novelty lies in the dataset and task specialization rather than a fundamentally new ranking algorithm.
The paper does not clearly state that SweLoc or the trained models/code will be publicly released, which is a significant reproducibility concern for a dataset-centric contribution.

The retriever loss may treat other positive functions from the same issue/PR as negatives if multiple instances from the same issue appear in a batch; this false-negative issue is not discussed or ablated.

Potential benchmark leakage is not fully addressed: the paper excludes SWE-Bench and LocBench repositories from training, but later evaluates on SWE-Bench Multilingual without mentioning whether those repositories were excluded.

The LLM reranker is described as listwise, but training only supervises the first generated identifier and omits the end-of-sequence token; this may limit learning of full ranking behavior, despite strong empirical results.
No statistical significance tests or variance estimates are reported for the main results, making it unclear how robust the gains are to run-to-run variation.
Ethical and licensing considerations for training on public GitHub issues, such as privacy, license compliance, or sensitive content, are not discussed.
